{{Short description|American experimental physicist}}
'''Blayne Ryan Heckel''' (born March 20, 1953) is an American experimental physicist whose research involved precision measurements in atomic physics and gravitational physics. He is a professor emeritus at the [[University of Washington]] in Seattle.

==Education and career==
At [[Harvard University]] he graduated with an A.B. in 1975 and a Ph.D. in 1981. His doctoral dissertation was supervised by [[Norman Ramsey]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Harvard PhD Theses in Physics: 1971–2000|website=Department of Physics, Harvard University|url=https://www.physics.harvard.edu/academics/phds1971-2000#y1980}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Blayne Heckel|website=Physics Tree|url=https://academictree.org/physics/tree.php?pid=115293&fontsize=0&pnodecount=4&cnodecount=2}}</ref> Heckel became an assistant professor in 1983, an associate professor in 1987, and a full professor in 1991 at the University of Washington,<ref name=aps2008elections>{{cite web|title=2008 Election: Candidate Information, Vice Chair|website=Topical Group on Precision Measurements & Fundamental Constants, American Physical Society|url=https://engage.aps.org/gpmfc/governance/candidates08}}</ref> where he was temporarily head of the physics department. Heckel founded there with [[Eric Adelberger]] in 1986 a group for experimental gravitational physics (Eöt-Wash Group), which [[Jens H. Gundlach]] joined in 1990. They further developed torsion balances in the style of [[Loránd Eötvös|Eötvös]] and used them to study the possible deviation of the [[gravitational force]] from Newton's <math>F = G \frac{m_1 m_2}{r^2}</math> law at small distances <math>r</math> (up to 50 micrometers). The Eöt-Wash group searched for possible new fundamental forces involving a [[fifth force]], large [[extra dimensions]], or the effects of [[dark matter]] and [[dark energy]], as well as possible violations of the [[equivalence principle]] at small distances. Heckel and his colleagues also used the torsion balance to test Lorentz invariance with polarized electrons and to look for new spin-dependent forces.

In the 1980s his research dealt with experimental atomic physics, including searches for [[Parity (physics)#Parity violation|violations of parity]] and violation of time reversal invariance, by means of measuring upper limits for the electric dipole moment of atoms such as [[Mercury (element)#Isotopes|<sup>199</sup>Hg]]. He worked with his doctoral advisor Norman Ramsey, among others.<ref>{{cite web|title=Norman Ramsey, Publications|website=Physics Tree|url=https://academictree.org/physics/peopleinfo.php?pid=2017}}</ref>

Heckel and his colleagues also measured the coupling constants of the [[weak interaction]] of neutrons with nucleons. His team used beams of cold polarized neutrons from the [[National Institute of Standards and Technology]] (NIST) reactor to bombard a [[liquid helium]] target, measuring the parity-violating spin of the beam polarization.<ref name=aps2008elections/>

In 2012 he was elected a member of the Washington State Academy of Sciences (WSAS).<ref>{{cite web | url=https://phys.washington.edu/news/2012/08/03/26-uw-selected-state-academy-sciences-includes-ann-nelson-james-bardeen-and-blayne | title=26 from UW selected for state Academy of Sciences, includes Ann Nelson, James Bardeen and Blayne Heckel &#124; Department of Physics &#124; University of Washington }}</ref> In 2021 he was awarded, jointly with Eric Adelberger and Jens H. Gundlach, the [[Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics]] for "precision fundamental measurements that test our understanding of gravity, probe the nature of [[dark energy]], and establish limits on couplings to [[dark matter]]."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://breakthroughprize.org/News/60|title=Breakthrough Prize – Winners Of The 2021 Breakthrough Prizes In Life Sciences, Fundamental Physics And Mathematics Announced|website=breakthroughprize.org}}</ref>

His doctoral students include [[Christopher Stubbs]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Christopher W. Stubbs|website=Physics Tree|url=https://academictree.org/physics/peopleinfo.php?pid=115291}}</ref>
